body.objective: Students will be able to play concert scales.
successCriteria: I can play the concert B♭, E♭ and F major scales
I can explain how a major scale is built
I can play scales with good tone and even rhythm
body.hook: Professional musicians warm up with scales every day. It's not just tradition: scales train your fingers, your ears and your sense of key all at once. Most of the music your band plays is built from these patterns.

vocabulary.definition: A series of notes moving step by step from one note to the same note an octave higher or lower.
A scale with the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.
A distance of two half steps on the keyboard.
The smallest distance between two notes in Western music.
The pitch as it sounds on a piano; many band instruments read different notes for the same sound.
The distance from one note to the next note with the same name.

study.title: Scale Builders
study.question: How are scales built, and why do musicians practise them?
study.passage:
The major scale pattern: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half (W W H W W W H).
Concert B♭ major: B♭ C D E♭ F G A B♭
Concert E♭ major: E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C D E♭
Concert F major: F G A B♭ C D E F
Transposing instruments: When the band plays concert B♭, B♭ instruments (clarinet, trumpet, tenor saxophone, baritone treble clef) read C major; E♭ instruments (alto and baritone saxophone) read G major; French horn in F reads F major; flute, oboe, trombone, euphonium, tuba and mallets read B♭ major. Check your scale sheet.
Part 1, Build (10 minutes): On a keyboard diagram, mark whole and half steps and build concert B♭ major using W W H W W W H.
Part 2, Play (15 minutes): Play each scale in whole notes, then half notes, then quarter notes at a metronome setting of 72. Focus on steady air and matching tone across the band.
Part 3, Scale games (10 minutes): "Echo": the teacher plays a pattern from the scale, the band echoes. "Scale in thirds": play 1-3, 2-4, 3-5 and so on.
Part 4, Self-check: record yourself on one scale and listen for even rhythm, tone and correct notes.
